findings: Background

Chapter 22 of the 3rd edition, Recognizing Text in Images, teaches PyTesseract and the Tesseract OCR engine (four lines to read an image, preprocessing advice, a large language model to fix mistakes, other languages) and the NAPS2 application run from Python for PDFs with embedded text, and ends with 7 practice questions and 1 practice program, the Browser Text Scraper [P01]. The page was fetched on 2026-10-13 and returned 200 with 40,521 bytes, holds 8 listings and 2 figures, and its sha256 equals the chapterDigest the book's own chapter ontology records [P01] [P03] [P04].
Errors a spell checker cannot see

The 2 wrong words of the 106 on Figure 22-1 (IT as In, motion as Motion) are real English words and a spell check against the 104,334 words of /usr/share/dict/words flagged nothing; the mean confidence was 94.5, the wrong In had 55 and Motion 92; the language model step was NOT EXECUTED, and its sample prompt has 419 characters [P01].
Hyphens at the line ends

ocr-example.png gave 51 lines with 7 words hyphenated at a line end (dig-ital, pro-grams, compre-hend, pro-grams, straight-forward, pro-gramming and graph-ics); removing every hyphen at a line end turned the real compound well-known into wellknown in a sample, so a word list is needed [P01].
Interpreters and releases

One program of 19 items printed the same under 11 interpreters (Python 3.11.17 to 3.15.0b4); 9 items printed the same under 14 Pillow releases (9.5.0 to 12.3.0); between pytesseract 0.3.9, 0.3.10 and 0.3.13 only the confidence type changed, a str in 0.3.9 and an int from 0.3.10 [P19] [P44] [P50].
Language codes

The chapter calls the language strings ISO 639-3 codes while the Tesseract manual page says ISO 639-2; 13 of the 126 names of tessdata_fast are not three letters, osd is no language, lang='ger' (the bibliographic 639-2 code of German) raises TesseractError while lang='deu' reads, lang='Japanese' raises the same error, and a missing pack inside 'eng+xyz' raises nothing and reads at 0.0116 [P01] [P14] [P31] [P32].
NAPS2

NAPS2 8.5.1 (the .deb package) ran the book's call with naps2_path = ['naps2', 'console'] (return code 0, 1 page, text error rate 0.0035) with its own Tesseract 5.5.0; a second call without -f returned 0 and printed File already exists. Use --force to overwrite.; the Windows path and flatpak raised FileNotFoundError; -i spam.pdf[0:2], spam.pdf[-2:] and spam.pdf[1:6:2] gave the pages 0 and 1, 5 and 6, and 1, 3 and 5 (MEASURED single run with the Tesseract version 5.5.0) [P01] [P22] [P23].
Not executed

Nothing ran on Windows or macOS, with Homebrew, with the Flatpak of NAPS2, with a flatbed scanner, with a large language model or on a real screen with a real browser; Python 3.15 was only a beta (3.15.0b4); the repository commit the course pins was not opened; and the photograph of the stories was not fetched because the single request to Wikimedia Commons answered 429 [P01] [P23] [P50].
Searchable PDFs

A PDF that Pillow made from frankenstein.png held 0 characters of text, the PDF of image_to_pdf_or_hocr read at 0.0138 with 106 word boxes, and ocrmypdf 17.13.0 exited 2 for a PNG without a resolution, 0 with --image-dpi 150 (0.0035), 6 for a PDF that already has text and 0 with --skip-text (MEASURED single runs with the Tesseract version 5.3.4) [P24] [P25].
Segmentation

--psm 3, 4, 6 and 11 read a page of 6 lines at 0.0116 and --psm 7 and 13 at 0.9923 and 0.9961; two columns read column by column with the default mode and merged line by line with --psm 6, and columns 2 and 4 pixels apart merged at 0.5819 and 0.5791; tesseract --help-psm lists 14 modes, and the chapter uses none of the words psm, dpi, whitelist or timeout (MEASURED single runs with the Tesseract version 5.3.4) [P01] [P14].
The Japanese page

On frankenstein_jpn.png (1211 by 606, 13 lines) the picture shows 第 5 章 and 憂鬱; the apt Tesseract with lang='jpn' printed 第 5 剖 and 愛鬱 where the book prints 第 5 剖 and 芝鬱, the fast data under 5.5.3 equalled the book and the best data gave 901 characters against 538; lang='eng' gave 0 Japanese characters and gibberish, and 'eng+jpn' read a mixed line correctly [P01].
The chapter replayed

Of the 22 statements of the chapter's listings 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 replayed as printed, 18 matched the book with the apt Tesseract 5.3.4, 20 with 5.5.3 and the fast data, 20 with 4.1.1, 18 with 5.5.3 and the best data, 19 with all the apt languages and 21 with all languages under 5.5.3; with the book's pins, 18 matched on Python 3.13.14, 8 on Python 3.14.6 and 0 in an empty Python; the statements that differ are get_languages(), the first word Iv, the Japanese heading and the English gibberish [P01] [P05].
The online materials

The online materials of the 3rd edition (7,759,877 bytes, 91 files, 72 of them Python) hold ocr-example.png (939 by 1198, mode RGBA), frankenstein.png (1130 by 672, mode P), frankenstein_jpn.png (1211 by 606, mode RGB) and preprocess_ocr.py (190 lines), and none of ocrscreen.py, output.pdf, cat.png, dog.png, moose.png, spam.pdf, eggs.pdf or output.txt, which the chapter creates or assumes; the publisher's book page has 1 occurrence of Recognizing Text and 0 of Tesseract, OCR or NAPS2 [P01] [P02] [P04].
The pin that cannot import

Appendix A pins pytesseract==0.3.10, whose source imports pkgutil.find_loader, removed in Python 3.14, so on Python 3.14.6 the import raises ImportError (cannot import name 'find_loader' from 'pkgutil'), on 3.13.14 it only warns, and 0.3.13 has no find_loader; PyPI has 28 releases of pytesseract, none numbered 0.3.11 or 0.3.12, and three older ones (0.3.4, 0.3.7 and 0.3.8) install only from source [P05] [P19] [P28].
The same page, different engines

The first word of frankenstein.png came back as Iv with 4.1.1 and 5.5.3 and the fast data, In with the apt 5.3.4, Ir with the best data of all three and It with the legacy data under 4.1.1 and 5.5.3, where the book prints Iv; the character error rate against the page was 0.0035 with the fast data and 0.0017 with the best and the legacy data (MEASURED single runs with the Tesseract versions named); the picture shows an I followed by a small capital T [P01] [P10] [P16] [P17].
The screen scraper

On a virtual X display the template's own constants (400, 200, 1000, 800) cropped 600 by 600 pixels and appended 361 characters (0.3824 against the page), the whole window gave 581 characters at 0.0035 and a second run made 1162 in all; without DISPLAY the import raised KeyError: 'DISPLAY'; nobody saw the screen (MEASURED single runs with the Tesseract version 5.3.4) [P01] [P33].
The shipped script and the linked post

preprocess_ocr.py (190 lines) calls FileNotFileError, grayscale_image and open_image, which it never defines, defines a function named open, and ends with NameError: name 'open_image' is not defined when run; the post at autbor.com/preprocessingocr answered 301 and then 200 and says it is a placeholder [P01] [P02] [P41].
The three kinds of English data

eng.traineddata is 4,113,088 bytes in tessdata_fast, 15,400,601 in tessdata_best and 23,466,654 in tessdata, each equal to the file its GitHub repository serves on 2026-10-13, and the apt package's file is the fast one; all of tessdata_fast is 706,776,225 bytes (126 languages and 37 script models), where the chapter says all languages add about 600MB [P01] [P10] [P16] [P17].
What helps

Enlarging a 9-pixel page 2 times lowered the error rate from 0.0579 to 0.0154, deskewing a page turned by 6 degrees (estimated -6.0) from 0.5985 to 0.0116, Otsu thresholding raised 0.0154 to 0.0347 on a noisy page, a tight crop returned the empty string and the same crop with a 10-pixel white border returned the line, and telling the engine 300 dpi for a 9-pixel page raised 0.0579 to 0.7452 (MEASURED single runs with the Tesseract version 5.3.4) [P01] [P08] [P43].
What hurts

On drawn pages with known text the apt Tesseract read 8-pixel letters at 0.2278 and 12-pixel letters at 0.0193, a page turned by 2 degrees at 0.0154 and by 5 degrees at 0.5753, noise of deviation 60 at 0.1313 and of 90 at 1.0 (MEASURED single runs with the Tesseract version 5.3.4); white text on black read at 0.0116 because tessedit_do_invert is 1 (deprecated, to go in release 6) and at 1.0965 with it off, so the chapter's advice of dark text on light describes what the engine did not need [P01] [P08].

nodes.label: Installing the tools
nodes.body: The first part of the chapter, Installing Tesseract and PyTesseract, tells the reader to install the free Tesseract OCR engine on Windows, macOS or Linux, optionally with language packs, and then the PyTesseract package, which also installs Pillow (Sweigart, 2025). The Tesseract documentation describes the engine as a command line program that is installed with apt on Linux, with brew on macOS and with an installer from UB Mannheim on Windows (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026).

paras.text: The first part of the chapter, Installing Tesseract and PyTesseract, tells the reader to install the free Tesseract OCR engine on Windows, macOS or Linux, optionally with language packs, and then the PyTesseract package, which also installs Pillow (Sweigart, 2025). The Tesseract documentation describes the engine as a command line program that is installed with apt on Linux, with brew on macOS and with an installer from UB Mannheim on Windows (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026).

Three ideas carry this subject: the engine (its version, its data folder and how pytesseract finds the program), the wrapper (the pytesseract release, the Python versions and the coupling with Pillow) and the installers of the three platforms. This study ran on Ubuntu 24.04 with the apt Tesseract 5.3.4 and its English data, pytesseract 0.3.13, Pillow 12.3.0 and Python 3.14.6 installed with uv; the Windows installer, the macOS installer and Homebrew were NOT EXECUTED (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: The engine
nodes.body: The chapter says PyTesseract works with the Tesseract OCR engine, a separate program that must be installed first, and that on Windows its folder must be on the PATH so that PyTesseract can reach tesseract.exe (Sweigart, 2025). The Tesseract command line documentation lists the options --version and --list-langs of that program (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026).

The Tesseract command line documentation lists the options --version and --list-langs of that program (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026).

Three leaves cover it: the version line, the data folder with the list of installed languages, and the way pytesseract looks the program up. The version of the engine matters because the same page gave different mistakes under Tesseract 4.1.1, 5.3.4 and 5.5.3 in this study (This study, 2026).

nodes.body: The chapter never prints the version of Tesseract it used; it says only that the exact results may vary as the language packs are updated (Sweigart, 2025). Wikipedia's article says version 4, released in 2018, added the LSTM-based engine, and version 5 was released in 2021 (Wikipedia, 2026).

nodes.body: The chapter says that on Windows the installation folder must be added to the PATH variable so PyTesseract can access tesseract.exe, and that Chapter 12 covered the PATH (Sweigart, 2025). The pytesseract README says that when the executable is not on the PATH, the variable pytesseract.pytesseract.tesseract_cmd names it (Pytesseract contributors, 2026).

paras.text: The chapter says that on Windows the installation folder must be added to the PATH variable so PyTesseract can access tesseract.exe, and that Chapter 12 covered the PATH (Sweigart, 2025). The pytesseract README says that when the executable is not on the PATH, the variable pytesseract.pytesseract.tesseract_cmd names it (Pytesseract contributors, 2026).

The default value of tesseract_cmd was the bare name 'tesseract', which shutil.which found at /usr/bin/tesseract; setting it to r'C:\Program Files\Tesseract-OCR\tesseract.exe', a well-formed Windows path (ntpath.isabs gave True), raised TesseractNotFoundError on this Linux machine (This study, 2026). The same error is what a reader sees on any system when the PATH entry is missing.

On ocr-example.png the apt Tesseract returned 51 lines, 10 of them blank lines between paragraphs, and 7 words broken at a line end by a hyphen: dig-ital, pro-grams, compre-hend, pro-grams, straight-forward, pro-gramming and graph-ics (This study, 2026). nodes.label: Accuracy and preprocessing
nodes.body: The part Preprocessing an Image warns that OCR text is always imperfect and lists nine preprocessing steps: separate columns, typewritten text, conventional fonts, upright lines, dark text on a light background, no dark borders, a small white border, enough contrast and no noise pixels; it points to a blog post on OpenCV (Sweigart, 2025). The Tesseract documentation page on quality has sections on rescaling, binarisation, noise removal, dilation and erosion, rotation and deskewing, and borders (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026).

paras.text: The part Preprocessing an Image warns that OCR text is always imperfect and lists nine preprocessing steps: separate columns, typewritten text, conventional fonts, upright lines, dark text on a light background, no dark borders, a small white border, enough contrast and no noise pixels; it points to a blog post on OpenCV (Sweigart, 2025). The Tesseract documentation page on quality has sections on rescaling, binarisation, noise removal, dilation and erosion, rotation and deskewing, and borders (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026).

Five ideas carry this subject: measuring accuracy (edit distance, character and word error rates), what hurts (small letters, typefaces, tilt, noise, low contrast, white on black), what helps (grey, thresholds, enlarging, a border, deskewing), how the page is segmented (psm) and the configuration strings. Every error rate below is for a page the program drew with known text and read with the apt Tesseract 5.3.4: MEASURED single runs with the Tesseract version 5.3.4 (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Measuring accuracy
nodes.body: The chapter has no measure of accuracy; it says OCR output is imperfect and should be corrected and that mistakes in numbers are harder to spot than misspelled words (Sweigart, 2025). The character error rate is the Levenshtein edit distance divided by the length of the reference, and the word error rate is the same quotient over words (Wikipedia, 2026).

paras.text: The chapter has no measure of accuracy; it says OCR output is imperfect and should be corrected and that mistakes in numbers are harder to spot than misspelled words (Sweigart, 2025). The character error rate is the Levenshtein edit distance divided by the length of the reference, and the word error rate is the same quotient over words (Wikipedia, 2026).

Three leaves define the measures used in every later number: the edit distance, the character error rate after white space is normalised, and the word error rate. They are a few lines of the study's own code, not a library, and they were checked on frankenstein.png, whose text was read from the picture (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Edit distance
nodes.body: Wikipedia's article on the Levenshtein distance defines it as the minimum number of single-character edits (insertions, deletions or substitutions) that change one word into the other and uses kitten and sitting as its example (Wikipedia, 2026). The Python documentation of difflib offers SequenceMatcher for aligning two sequences (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Wikipedia's article on the Levenshtein distance defines it as the minimum number of single-character edits (insertions, deletions or substitutions) that change one word into the other and uses kitten and sitting as its example (Wikipedia, 2026). The Python documentation of difflib offers SequenceMatcher for aligning two sequences (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The study's lev() gave 3 for kitten and sitting, 3 for the empty string and abc, 0 for equal strings, and 1 for It against Iv and for In against IT, the two kinds of mistake in the chapter's listing (This study, 2026). The distance between In and IT is 1 because only the second letter differs.

nodes.definition: The edit distance counts the insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn one string into another: kitten to sitting is 3, an empty string to abc is 3, equal strings 0, It to Iv 1 and In to IT 1.

nodes.label: Character error rate
nodes.body: A rate needs a reference. The study divides the edit distance by the number of characters of the reference after every run of white space has become one space, so that line breaks do not count as errors (This study, 2026). The Wikipedia article on word error rate gives the same quotient for words (Wikipedia, 2026).

paras.text: A rate needs a reference. The study divides the edit distance by the number of characters of the reference after every run of white space has become one space, so that line breaks do not count as errors (This study, 2026). The Wikipedia article on word error rate gives the same quotient for words (Wikipedia, 2026).

abcd read as abxd gave 0.25; 'a  b' and 'c' on two lines against 'a b c' gave 0.0; an empty reading of abcd gave 1.0, and so did abcd read as abcdefgh, because the quotient reaches 1.0 when the output is twice as long and can pass it (white text on black without inversion gave 1.0965) (This study, 2026). A rate of 1.0 therefore means nothing useful was read, not that every character was wrong.

nodes.definition: The character error rate is the edit distance divided by the length of the reference after white space is normalised: abcd against abxd is 0.25, an empty reading is 1.0 and a longer reading is 1.0 for abcd against abcdefgh.

nodes.label: Word error rate
nodes.body: The word error rate counts words; the Wikipedia article gives it as the substitutions, deletions and insertions over the number of words in the reference (Wikipedia, 2026). The chapter counts mistakes only by eye, naming Iv and Motion (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The word error rate counts words; the Wikipedia article gives it as the substitutions, deletions and insertions over the number of words in the reference (Wikipedia, 2026). The chapter counts mistakes only by eye, naming Iv and Motion (Sweigart, 2025).

'The cat sat' read as 'the cat sit' and as 'the cat' gave 1 of 3 words each, 0.3333; frankenstein.png has 106 words, 2 of them wrong, so its word error rate was 0.0189 against a character error rate of 0.0035, because one wrong letter spoils a whole word (MEASURED single run with the Tesseract version 5.3.4) (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: What hurts
nodes.body: The chapter says Tesseract is designed for typewritten dark text on light backgrounds where the text is level, that photographs and handwriting are out of reach, and that cursive and stylized fonts, tilt, noise and white text on black should be avoided (Sweigart, 2025). The Tesseract quality page lists scale, skew, noise and borders among the causes of poor results (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026).

paras.text: The chapter says Tesseract is designed for typewritten dark text on light backgrounds where the text is level, that photographs and handwriting are out of reach, and that cursive and stylized fonts, tilt, noise and white text on black should be avoided (Sweigart, 2025). The Tesseract quality page lists scale, skew, noise and borders among the causes of poor results (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026).

Six leaves cover it: letter size, typeface, tilt, noise, low contrast and white text on black. Each drew a text of 259 characters (the opening of the Frankenstein paragraph) with Pillow and read it with the apt Tesseract 5.3.4: MEASURED single runs with the Tesseract version 5.3.4 (This study, 2026). Looking at the drawn pages, the tilted, the noisy and the 8-pixel pages are all readable by eye, so the engine's limits are not a human's (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Small text
nodes.body: The Tesseract quality page says the engine works best on images of at least 300 dpi, so it may help to resize them (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026). The chapter does not mention size or resolution (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The Tesseract quality page says the engine works best on images of at least 300 dpi, so it may help to resize them (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026). The chapter does not mention size or resolution (Sweigart, 2025).

On a 700-pixel page of DejaVu Sans the error rate was 0.2278 at 8 pixels, 0.0309 at 10, 0.0193 at 12 and 0.0116 at 16 and at 24 pixels; on a 900-pixel page 6 pixels gave 1.0 (nothing read) and 8 pixels 0.2394 (MEASURED single runs with the Tesseract version 5.3.4) (This study, 2026). The letters of a screenshot are small, so the screen scraper of the practice program needs one more rule: enlarge before reading.

nodes.label: Font choice
nodes.body: The chapter says to use conventional fonts, not cursive or stylized fonts (Sweigart, 2025). Kurzweil's company, founded in 1974, built the first omni-font OCR system, which Wikipedia describes as able to recognize text in any normal font (Wikipedia, 2026).

paras.text: The chapter says to use conventional fonts, not cursive or stylized fonts (Sweigart, 2025). Kurzweil's company, founded in 1974, built the first omni-font OCR system, which Wikipedia describes as able to recognize text in any normal font (Wikipedia, 2026).

Six typefaces drawn at 24 pixels on a 900-pixel page read with error rates of 0.0116 (DejaVu Sans), 0.0 (DejaVu Serif), 0.0 (DejaVu Sans Mono), 0.0116 (DejaVu Sans Bold), 0.0 (Nimbus Roman) and 0.0 (Z003 italic script) (MEASURED single runs with the Tesseract version 5.3.4) (This study, 2026). So the advice to avoid stylized fonts did not matter for clean typeset faces of this size; it concerns handwriting and decoration, which were not measured.

A page turned by 2 degrees read at 0.0154, but 5 degrees gave 0.5753 and 10 and 20 degrees gave 1.0, against 0.0116 upright; on the 900-pixel page of the corpus program 3 degrees already gave 0.6409 (MEASURED single runs with the Tesseract version 5.3.4) (This study, 2026). So 'a slight angle' in the chapter means about two degrees; the picture of a page turned by 5 degrees is easily readable by eye.

Gaussian noise with a standard deviation of 30 grey levels left the error rate at 0.0116, 60 gave 0.1313 and 90 gave 1.0; on the 900-pixel page of the corpus program 50 gave 0.0154 and 60 gave 1.0 (MEASURED single runs with the Tesseract version 5.3.4) (This study, 2026). nodes.label: Low contrast
nodes.body: The chapter says to adjust the brightness and contrast of the image so that the text stands out from the background (Sweigart, 2025). The Tesseract quality page has a section on binarisation, the step that turns grey into black and white (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026).

paras.text: The chapter says to adjust the brightness and contrast of the image so that the text stands out from the background (Sweigart, 2025). The Tesseract quality page has a section on binarisation, the step that turns grey into black and white (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026).

In the corpus program grey 170 on 190 read as well as black on white (0.0116), but with light noise (a standard deviation of 12 grey levels) grey 100 on 160 read at 0.0656 while 110 on 140, 120 on 135 and 125 on 130 gave 1.0, against 0.0116 for black on white (MEASURED single runs with the Tesseract version 5.3.4) (This study, 2026). Contrast and noise together decide, not either alone.

nodes.body: The chapter says to use dark text on a light background, not white text on a black background (Sweigart, 2025). The Tesseract quality page says that for version 4.x one should use dark text on a light background (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026).

White text on black read at 0.0116 with the default settings, the same as black on white, because Tesseract tries an inverted line image (the parameter tessedit_do_invert is 1); with -c tessedit_do_invert=0 the error rate was 1.0965, and inverting the picture oneself and keeping the switch off gave 0.0116 again (MEASURED single runs with the Tesseract version 5.3.4) (This study, 2026). nodes.label: What helps
nodes.body: The chapter says some of the preprocessing steps can be performed automatically with Python using the OpenCV library, and points to the blog post Preprocessing Images for OCR with Python and OpenCV at autbor.com/preprocessingocr (Sweigart, 2025). PyPI lists opencv-python-headless 5.0.0.93 as the newest release, uploaded on 2026-07-02 (Python Package Index, 2026).

PyPI lists opencv-python-headless 5.0.0.93 as the newest release, uploaded on 2026-07-02 (Python Package Index, 2026).

Five leaves cover it: grey conversion, Otsu thresholding, enlarging, a white border and deskewing, done with Pillow, NumPy and OpenCV 5.0.0 on pages drawn by the program (MEASURED single runs with the Tesseract version 5.3.4) (This study, 2026). Not every step helped: thresholding made one page worse.

nodes.label: Grayscale conversion
nodes.body: The chapter's contrast step can be done with Pillow's ImageOps, whose reference lists autocontrast, invert, grayscale and expand (Pillow Developers, 2026). The chapter itself does not mention grey conversion (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The chapter's contrast step can be done with Pillow's ImageOps, whose reference lists autocontrast, invert, grayscale and expand (Pillow Developers, 2026). The chapter itself does not mention grey conversion (Sweigart, 2025).

convert('L') turned the colour pixel (167, 205, 128) into the grey 185 and left the error rate of a clean colour page at 0.0116, as before the conversion, so the engine did not need it; on the book's frankenstein.png the corpus program measured 0.0035 as shipped and 0.0017 after the grey conversion, and the first word changed from In to Iv (This study, 2026). A palette image such as that file (mode P) becomes a different picture to the engine when converted.

nodes.label: Binarization
nodes.body: Wikipedia says Otsu's method, published by Nobuyuki Otsu in 1979, chooses a threshold automatically from the grey histogram (Wikipedia, 2026). The Tesseract quality page says version 5.0.0 added the Leptonica-based Adaptive Otsu and Sauvola binarisation methods (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026).

paras.text: Wikipedia says Otsu's method, published by Nobuyuki Otsu in 1979, chooses a threshold automatically from the grey histogram (Wikipedia, 2026). The Tesseract quality page says version 5.0.0 added the Leptonica-based Adaptive Otsu and Sauvola binarisation methods (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026).

Otsu's threshold on a page with noise of 45 was 136.0 and left only the values 0 and 255, but the error rate rose from 0.0154 to 0.0347 (MEASURED single runs with the Tesseract version 5.3.4) (This study, 2026). In the corpus program the median filter of 3 pixels followed by Otsu gave 0.0116 on a page with noise of 60, where the unfiltered page gave 1.0, so the order of the steps matters.

nodes.label: White border
nodes.body: The chapter says to add a small white border if the text runs up against the edge of the image (Sweigart, 2025). The Tesseract quality page has a section called missing borders, which says text without any border may give problems (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026).

Text cropped tight to its ink (383 by 24 pixels) returned the empty string, and the same crop with a 10-pixel white border (403 by 44) returned 'Tesseract reads this line' with a newline (This study, 2026). In the corpus program a page drawn with a margin of 0 pixels still read at 0.0116, because its lines were not cut off, so the border rule matters for tight crops, such as those of the screen scraper.

OpenCV's minAreaRect of the dark pixels estimated the skew of a page turned by 6 degrees as -6.0 degrees; rotating back with Pillow lowered the error rate from 0.5985 to 0.0116 and enlarged the picture from 718 by 264 to 742 by 338 pixels (MEASURED single runs with the Tesseract version 5.3.4) (This study, 2026). In the corpus program the estimate was right for 3, 5 and 10 degrees and wrong for 30 (it found -20), where the result stayed at 1.0.

nodes.body: The chapter's rule is not to scan multicolumn images; its Summary says Tesseract works with typewritten dark text on light backgrounds where the text is level (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The chapter's rule is not to scan multicolumn images; its Summary says Tesseract works with typewritten dark text on light backgrounds where the text is level (Sweigart, 2025).

Two columns of 330 pixels placed 360 pixels apart on a 700-pixel page read with the default mode column by column (alpha beta gamma delta epsilon zeta eta theta iota kappa lam), while --psm 6 joined them line by line (alpha beta gamma delta one two three four five six epsilon); each column cut out and read alone had an error rate of 0.0 (This study, 2026). nodes.label: Whitelist digits
nodes.body: The Tesseract quality page names the parameter tessedit_char_whitelist as the way to limit the characters that are recognized (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026). The chapter says to pay special attention to mistakes in numbers (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The Tesseract quality page names the parameter tessedit_char_whitelist as the way to limit the characters that are recognized (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026). The chapter says to pay special attention to mistakes in numbers (Sweigart, 2025).

With -c tessedit_char_whitelist=0123456789- the line 'Order 4417-B shipped on 2026-10-13' became '4417-02026-10-13': the letters vanished and the B was read as a 0 (This study, 2026). In the corpus program a digits-only image '0123456789 0O8B 5S 1l 2Z 6G' read without the whitelist as '0123456789 008B 5S 1l 2Z 6G' and with it as '0123456789008855112266'. A whitelist removes look-alike letters by forcing digits, so it can also turn a wrong letter into a wrong digit.

nodes.label: Languages and data
nodes.body: The part Recognizing Text in Non-English Languages says Tesseract assumes English by default, lists the packs with tess.get_languages(), explains that the strings are mostly three-character ISO 639-3 language codes, passes lang='jpn' to read frankenstein_jpn.png, shows the gibberish of the wrong language and joins languages with a plus sign (Sweigart, 2025). The installation section adds that installing all languages takes about 600MB (Sweigart, 2025).

The installation section adds that installing all languages takes about 600MB (Sweigart, 2025).

Three ideas carry this subject: the packs (the list, the folder and the size), the choice of language (the codes, the Japanese page, the wrong language, combinations, a missing pack and accented letters) and the kinds of data (fast, best and legacy) with the engine modes. The apt package carries the tessdata_fast English file; tessdata_best and tessdata were cloned from their GitHub repositories and each file was compared with the one the repository serves today (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Iso codes
nodes.body: The chapter says the strings are mostly three-character ISO 639-3 codes with a few exceptions such as aze_cyrl, and the installation section says to use a three-character ISO 639 code such as fra, deu or jpn (Sweigart, 2025). The Tesseract manual page says the language is given as an ISO 639-2 code (Tesseract OCR contributors, 2026); ISO 639-3 is the SIL table and ISO 639-2 the Library of Congress list (SIL International, 2026)(Library of Congress, 2026).

lecture.title: Chapter 22: Reading Text from Images with OCR
lecture.say: This chapter is about reading the text out of a picture, which is called optical character recognition, or OCR. It has fifteen examples, and all of them run on the chapter page in the order of this deck. The pictures are drawn by the examples themselves, so no file has to be downloaded. Part 1 installs the engine and reads a first line. Part 2 measures what makes a reading fail. Part 3 repairs pictures and names languages. Part 4 finds mistakes, writes a searchable PDF and calls a scanner program. Part 5 reads the screen and ends with the practice program. Slide 2 gives the route through the parts.

lecture.title: Today's route through five parts
lecture.say: The chapter has five parts. Part 1 explains the two pieces that OCR needs, the program Tesseract and the module pytesseract, and reads a line, several lines and single words. Part 2 measures three limits: the height of the text, the tilt of the page and the noise on the picture. Part 3 repairs pictures, narrows a reading with settings and reads German and French. Part 4 compares a reading with a known text, writes a PDF and calls NAPS2. Part 5 reads a region of the screen and loops over pages. Each range on the slide is a run of slides you can jump to. Slide 3 gives the two questions that the parts answer.

lecture.title: Two questions this chapter answers
lecture.say: Two questions frame the chapter. The first asks which properties of a picture decide whether Tesseract can read it, and how far each can go. Part 2 answers it with three measured limits, and the summary repeats them. The second asks how a program reads a region of the screen, keeps the text and notices when the reading went wrong. Part 4 gives the way to notice mistakes and part 5 gives the screen loop. The practice slide lets you check yourself on both questions. The answers come back on slide 37.

lecture.title: Part 1: The engine and the first reading
lecture.say: Part 1 starts with the two pieces that OCR needs. Tesseract is a separate program that does the reading, and pytesseract is a small Python module that hands it a picture and returns the text. The part then reads one line with image_to_string(), reads three lines and looks at the single str that comes back, and finally asks for every word with its position and its confidence. Slide 7 shows how to check that the engine is installed and which languages it knows.

lecture.title: Installing Tesseract and pytesseract
lecture.say: Reading text from a picture needs two parts. Tesseract is a program, installed with an installer on Windows and macOS or with the package manager on Linux. pytesseract is a Python module, installed with pip, which only sends the picture to Tesseract and returns the answer. If the program is missing, the module raises an error. get_languages() lists the language files that are installed, and English is always among them. The book also uses the NAPS2 scanner, which needs its own English data. Slide 7 shows the version and the language list.

lecture.title: Story: A machine of 1931 searched microfilm by recognizing patterns
lecture.say: In 1931 the engineer Emanuel Goldberg was granted US patent 1,838,389 for his Statistical Machine. It searched rolls of microfilm with photoelectric cells and pattern recognition, so it matched shapes without a person reading them. The picture shows the memorial stone laid for him in Dresden, which gives his birth year, 1881, his flight in 1933 to France and his move in 1937 to Palestine. The idea of finding the shapes of characters by machine is the same as that of Tesseract. Slide 7 shows how the engine is called from Python.

lecture.title: Is the engine installed, and which languages does it know?
lecture.say: The first printed line is the version of Tesseract that ran, 5.3.4. The second line says that 22 language files are installed and shows the first five: ara, chi_sim, chi_tra, deu and eng. The last line is True for eng and False for xyz, which means the English file is installed and a file named xyz is not. pytesseract does not read anything itself: it starts the program Tesseract, so a missing program is the first thing to check when a reading fails. Slide 24 uses deu and fra from the same list.

lecture.title: OCR fundamentals and the first reading
lecture.say: Optical character recognition turns a picture of text into text. In pytesseract the central call is image_to_string(), which takes a picture, either an Image object made by Pillow or one opened with Image.open(), and returns everything that was read as a single str. The book uses a four-line picture, ocr-example.png, and a scan of a printed page from an 1831 print of Frankenstein, shown as its Figure 22-1. The next slides read pictures that the examples draw themselves, so they need no download. Slide 9 reads the first line.

lecture.title: Reading one line with image_to_string()
lecture.say: The printed result is 'Hello OCR 2026' followed by a line break, and the second line says True: after strip() the text equals the sentence that was drawn. The picture is drawn by the example, black text on a white ground, 440 by 90 pixels, with the font that Pillow itself carries. image_to_string() returns a str, and Tesseract always ends it with a line break, so strip() is the usual second step. Reading clear text in a large size is the easy case; the next examples make it harder. Slide 10 reads several lines in one call.

lecture.title: Lines, line breaks and the answer's type
lecture.say: The picture has three lines, and image_to_string() returned one str of 83 characters for all of them. splitlines() shows what was read: the second line contains a vertical bar where the word 'I' stood, so Tesseract made a mistake even on clean text, and an empty string appears between the second and the third line, which is the blank line that Tesseract inserts. A program that uses the text must expect both. Part 4 shows how to find such mistakes by comparing with the truth. Compare slide 11, which asks for each word and its position.

lecture.title: Words with boxes and confidence: image_to_data()
lecture.say: image_to_data() returns, for the same line, a dictionary of lists: the word, its confidence and its position. The four words are Invoice, 2026-114, total and 482.50, each with a confidence of 96 out of 100, and the left and top numbers show where each word stands: 23, 133, 281 and 352 pixels from the left. Empty entries, which stand for lines and blocks, are skipped with strip(). A program can use the confidence to decide which words to check by hand, and the position to crop a word. See slide 28 for the use of such results in finding mistakes.

lecture.title: Part 2: What makes reading fail
lecture.say: Part 2 asks what makes a reading fail. A program that reads text from pictures is only useful if you know where it stops working, so each example changes one property of the same sentence and prints a score from 0 to 1. The properties are the height of the text, the tilt of the page and the noise on the picture. The comparison table on slide 18 collects the three limits that the runs found, together with the repairs that part 3 tests.

lecture.title: Preparing a picture for reading
lecture.say: Preprocessing means changing a picture before it is read, so that the reading improves. The usual changes are turning a tilted page back, enlarging text that is too small, removing noise and reducing the picture to black and white. Not every change helps: the examples of part 2 first find where a reading fails, and the first example of part 3 tests two repairs and one that made a reading worse. Each change should be tested on the same picture and compared by a score. Slide 18 collects the limits.

lecture.title: Story: The first reading machine for blind people was unveiled in 1976
lecture.say: Ray Kurzweil founded Kurzweil Computer Products in 1974 to build OCR that could read any typeface and not only one fixed font. The reading machine for blind people, which scanned a page and read it aloud, was unveiled on 13 January 1976. The story belongs before part 2 because such a machine also needed a good picture: the next slides measure how small, how crooked and how noisy a picture may be before Tesseract fails.

lecture.title: How small can the text be?
lecture.say: The loop prints a score for each text height. At 7 and 8 pixels the reading is empty and the score is 0.0; at 9 pixels it is 0.95; at 10 pixels it is 0.99; and from 12 pixels it is 1.0. The score is the similarity of the reading to the sentence that was drawn, from difflib. A text smaller than about 9 pixels cannot be read, which is why scans are made at a high resolution. The repair, enlarging the picture, is tested in part 3. Compare slides 16 and 17, which change the tilt and the noise instead.

lecture.title: How crooked can the page be?
lecture.say: The same sentence is turned by an angle. At 0 and 4 degrees the score is 1.0, at 6 degrees 0.98, at 7 degrees 0.9, at 8 degrees 0.91, and at 9 and 12 degrees the reading is empty or wrong: 0.0 and 0.25. A page that is scanned crookedly by less than about 8 degrees is still read, and a page tilted more must be turned back first. The first example of part 3 turns a picture back and measures the gain. See slide 22 for the repair.

lecture.title: How much noise can the picture carry?
lecture.say: NumPy adds a random value between minus s and plus s to every pixel, and the loop prints the score for six values of s. Up to 100 the score is 1.0; at 105 and above the reading is empty. The change is abrupt: the text is read perfectly or not at all, so a program should check its result and not rely on the noise being small. The noise here is uniform random noise; a scan has other kinds, such as stains, and they need other repairs. Compare slide 15 and slide 16; slide 18 puts the three limits together.

lecture.title: Three limits of a reading, measured by the run
lecture.say: The table collects the three limits that the runs of this part measured and the repairs that were tested. The text must be at least 9 pixels high, the page may be tilted up to 8 degrees, and the noise may reach 100. A tilted page is repaired completely by turning it back, small text is repaired by enlarging it three times, and no repair for noise was found in these examples. Every number in the table was measured by the program when this deck was built, with Tesseract 5.3.4 and one font. See slides 15, 16 and 17 for the runs behind the numbers.

lecture.title: Part 3: Cleaning, settings and languages
lecture.say: Part 3 repairs and steers a reading. The first example turns a tilted picture back and enlarges a small one, and it also shows that reducing a picture to black and white can make a reading worse, so every step needs a test. The second example gives Tesseract settings: a page mode that says one line, and a whitelist of the characters that may appear. The third reads German and French with the language files that name them, and shows the error of a language that is not installed.

lecture.title: Languages other than English
lecture.say: Tesseract reads English unless it is told otherwise. For another language you install its language file and pass the code with lang=, for example lang='deu' for German. Two files can be joined with a plus sign, as in lang='eng+jpn'. The book's example reads a page with Japanese text, frankenstein_jpn.png. With only the English file, an accented letter is read as another letter, and a language that is not installed raises an error. Slide 24 shows both results.

lecture.title: Story: Tesseract began at Hewlett-Packard in 1985 and became open source
lecture.say: Tesseract was developed at Hewlett-Packard laboratories from 1985. Hewlett-Packard released it as open source in 2005, and Google sponsored its development from 2006. Because it is open source, other tools can offer it: the picture shows the transcription tool of Wikisource, where Tesseract OCR is one choice, set here to the Tamil script, and pytesseract does the same calling for Python. The slides that follow use version 5.3.4, and the language files that come with it, to read English, German and French. See also slide 7, where the version is printed.

lecture.title: Cleaning a picture before reading it
lecture.say: Three printed lines show three repairs. A page tilted by 10 degrees scores 0.0, and turned back by 10 degrees it scores 1.0. A text of 8 pixels scores 0.0, and enlarged three times with the LANCZOS filter it scores 0.98. The last line applies a black-and-white table with point() to the enlarged picture and the score falls to 0.7, so that step made the reading worse. A repair must be tested on the picture at hand; a step that helps one picture can hurt another. See slide 18 for the limits that these repairs address.

lecture.title: Page modes and a whitelist of characters
lecture.say: The first line is the reading without settings: Call 555-0199 now: 2026. The second line uses two settings in one string: --psm 7 tells Tesseract that the picture holds a single line, and tessedit_char_whitelist lists the only characters that may be returned. The result is 555-01992026, digits and the hyphen only, and the spaces and letters are gone. Settings are passed in the config argument. A whitelist suits fields such as telephone numbers, and it also makes a reading wrong when the field holds other characters.

lecture.title: Reading German and French with lang=
lecture.say: The same picture is read twice, once as English and once as its own language. For the German line the similarity to the truth rises from 0.83 to 1.0 with lang='deu', and for the French line from 0.86 to 1.0 with lang='fra'. The English file has no letters such as ü, ß or é, so it replaces them with similar ones. The last line shows that asking for a language that is not installed raises a TesseractError. The font DejaVu Sans is used because the font of Pillow has no accented letters. Slide 20 explains the language files.

lecture.title: Part 4: Mistakes, PDF and scanners
lecture.say: Part 4 is about what comes after a reading. A reading has mistakes, so the first example compares it with a known text and lists each difference, which is also the first step of any automatic correction, including one done by a language model. The second example writes a PDF whose invisible text layer can be searched. The third calls the scanner program NAPS2 from Python with subprocess, and shows what Python does when that program is not installed.

lecture.title: Mistakes, searchable PDFs and NAPS2
lecture.say: Three ideas of this part belong together. A reading has mistakes, and a language model can correct what remains, but the program must still check the correction against the source. NAPS2 is a free scanner program with a command line, and subprocess.run() starts any program with a list of arguments; check=True raises an error when the program fails. The arguments -i and -o name the input picture and the output file, and -n 0 scans no new page. OCRmyPDF is another program that adds an invisible text layer to a PDF. Slides 28, 29 and 30 hold the three examples.

lecture.title: Story: reCAPTCHA used what OCR could not read to digitize books
lecture.say: reCAPTCHA began at Carnegie Mellon University in a team around Luis von Ahn, and Google acquired it in September 2009. A visitor was shown two words: one that the program already knew and one that OCR had not been able to read. A correct answer to the known word gave weight to the answer for the other one, and the answers digitized books. The comparison with a known text is the idea of the next slides, which find the mistakes of a reading. Compare slide 28, which finds the mistakes of a reading.

lecture.title: Finding the mistakes of a reading
lecture.say: The example uses a reading with four typical mistakes: a lower-case l for a capital I, a capital O for a zero, a capital I for a lower-case l, and another O for a zero. get_opcodes() lists each place where the two texts differ, and the loop prints the true character and what was read. The last line is the similarity, 0.86. A program can use such a list to decide what to correct, whether by hand, by a rule or by a language model; the corrected text should be compared with the source again.

lecture.title: A searchable PDF from a picture
lecture.say: image_to_pdf_or_hocr() returns bytes, and they start with %PDF-, so the result is a PDF. It contains the picture and an invisible layer of the text that was read. The example writes the bytes to a file and starts pdftotext, another program, with subprocess.run(); the list it prints holds both lines of the page, so the text of the picture can be searched and copied. The extension argument can also be 'hocr' for a web page that keeps the position of every word.

lecture.title: Running the scanner program NAPS2 from Python
lecture.say: The first line prints the command as one string: NAPS2.Console -n 0 -i ocr-example.png -o output.pdf. The arguments are given to subprocess.run() as a list, one word each. NAPS2 is not installed on the machine that ran this example, so Python raises FileNotFoundError and the program prints its name and the missing file name, NAPS2.Console. The try statement turns a missing program into a message; with check=True a program that starts and fails raises a different error, CalledProcessError. Compare slide 29, which starts pdftotext in the same way.

lecture.title: Part 5: The screen and the practice program
lecture.say: Part 5 reads the screen. A screenshot is a picture, so everything of the earlier parts applies to it: crop it to the text, read it and keep the result. The first example uses an emulated screen, because the real screenshot function needs a display. The second example is the practice program of the chapter, a browser text scraper: for each page of a document it takes a screenshot, crops it, reads it and appends the text to a file. The questions after it let you check the whole chapter.

lecture.title: The screen and the practice program
lecture.say: pyautogui is a third-party module that controls the mouse, the keyboard and the screen. Its screenshot() function returns a picture of the screen as an Image, which can be cropped and read like any other picture. The book's Figure 22-2 shows a web page with an embedded document whose text cannot be copied, which is the case for the practice program, the browser text scraper. It reads each page of the document from a screenshot and appends the text to output.txt; the book's program is called ocrscreen.py. Slide 36 has the questions.

lecture.title: Story: The 1831 edition of Frankenstein is the page the book scans
lecture.say: Mary Shelley's Frankenstein appeared anonymously in 1818, and a revised edition of 1831 carries her name. The picture is the frontispiece engraving of that edition, made by Theodor von Holst and now in the public domain. The book's Figure 22-1 is a scan of a page of the same print, a hard case for OCR because of the age of the paper and the typeface. The screenshot of the next slides is the easy case, since screen text is sharp. See also slide 34, where a screenshot is read.

lecture.title: Reading text from the screen
lecture.say: The example draws its own screen, because the real screenshot function of pyautogui needs a display, and it says EMULATED. The screenshot is 640 by 300 pixels, and the crop keeps the region from row 50 to row 170, 640 by 120 pixels. Tesseract reads only that region and returns the lines Embedded document and Page 3 of 12: total 482.50 with an empty string between them. Cropping first removes the browser bar and everything else that is not text, which makes the reading faster and cleaner. See slide 35 for the loop that repeats it.

lecture.title: Practice program: a browser text scraper
lecture.say: The practice program of the chapter is a browser text scraper. The example draws three emulated pages of a document. For each page the loop takes a screenshot, crops it, reads it and appends the text and a line break to output.txt. The last line prints the file's three lines: Page 1 of 3: total 100.50, Page 2 of 3: total 200.50 and Page 3 of 3: total 300.50. In the book the pages are changed by pressing a key, which needs a display; the loop is the same. Compare slide 34, which reads one screenshot.

lecture.title: Practice Questions
lecture.say: These are the practice questions, and each points to the part where the idea was shown. The first is about the two installed parts and get_languages(), slide 7. The second is about the smallest text height that reads well, slide 15. The third is about the whitelist, slide 23. The fourth is about languages and the error of a missing one, slide 24. The fifth is about the scraper's loop, slide 35. Run the examples on the chapter page to check each answer.

lecture.title: Summary
lecture.say: Four sentences carry the chapter. pytesseract is a bridge to the program Tesseract, and image_to_string() returns a str. Size, tilt and noise each have a limit, and turning a page back and enlarging small text are repairs that work. lang= names the language, and the settings --psm and a whitelist narrow a reading. A reading should be compared with a known text, and a screenshot should be cropped to its text before it is read. Slides 3 and 36 give the two questions and the practice questions again.

lecture.title: Resources: where to go next
lecture.say: These fifteen links are where to go next. They include the chapter of the book, the documentation of Tesseract, pytesseract, NAPS2, OCRmyPDF and PyAutoGUI, the Python documentation for difflib and subprocess, and the pages behind the stories: Emanuel Goldberg, Kurzweil Computer Products, Tesseract, reCAPTCHA and Frankenstein. Each page shows the date on which it was opened. Use the documentation pages to find options that the examples do not use, such as other page modes. See also slide 3 for the two questions of the chapter.

examples.name: Finding the mistakes of a reading
examples.code:
import difflib
TRUTH = 'Invoice 2026-114 total 482.50'
read = 'lnvoice 2O26-114 totaI 482.5O'
for tag, i1, i2, j1, j2 in difflib.SequenceMatcher(None, TRUTH, read).get_opcodes():
    if tag != 'equal':
        print(tag, repr(TRUTH[i1:i2]), 'read as', repr(read[j1:j2]))
ratio = difflib.SequenceMatcher(None, TRUTH, read).ratio()
print(round(ratio, 2))
examples.note: This example runs in your browser and prints the same as the slide: four differences and the similarity 0.86.

examples.name: A searchable PDF
examples.code:
import subprocess, tempfile
import pytesseract as tess
# im holds two lines of text
pdf = tess.image_to_pdf_or_hocr(im, extension='pdf')
print(type(pdf).__name__, pdf[:5])
path = tempfile.mktemp(suffix='.pdf')
open(path, 'wb').write(pdf)
done = subprocess.run(['pdftotext', path, '-'], capture_output=True, text=True)

def screenshot(n):
    im = Image.new('RGB', (640, 160), 'white')
    line = f'Page {n} of 3: total {n * 100}.50'

examples.code:
def screenshot(n):
    im = Image.new('RGB', (640, 160), 'white')
    line = f'Page {n} of 3: total {n * 100}.50'
    ImageDraw.Draw(im).text((20, 50), line, fill='black', font=font)
    return im
for n in (1, 2, 3):
    part = screenshot(n).crop((0, 20, 640, 120))
    text = tess.image_to_string(part).strip()
    with open('output.txt', 'a') as f:
        f.write(text + '\n')
print(open('output.txt').read().splitlines())
